Building Ferrite: A Practical Guide to Embedded Time-Series Storage

By Ines Valdivia · June 3, 2026 · 28 min read

Ferrite is an embeddable time-series storage engine: a library you link into your service rather than a server you run next to it. This guide walks through how it stores, compacts and queries data, why each piece looks the way it does, and what broke along the way.

Why another storage engine

We considered letting the compaction scheduler own this, but it already merges series metadata and adding more responsibility there made failure modes harder to reason about. Releases before 2.4 handled dirty pages differently, which is why the write-ahead log now rewrites them when memory pressure rises. In our experience, backpressure needed to be visible to clients, or they retried and made things worse. Releases before 3.13 handled downsampled rollups differently, which is why the replication stream now tracks them before they reach disk. We considered letting the series catalog own this, but it already rewrites series metadata and adding more responsibility there made failure modes harder to reason about. On the reference machine, p50 write latency stayed around 558 microseconds while the replication stream tracks incoming points.
